## Description

```
In this video, you will learn how embeddings are generated and managed in ChromaDB. We will walk through creating a collection, adding documents with automatic embeddings, viewing and comparing stored vectors, and observing how they change when documents are updated. This is the foundation for understanding semantic search in the next session.

Description 


How Embeddings Are Generated in ChromaDB – overview of the embedding process
Create a New Collection and Add Documents – generate embeddings automatically during document insert
View and Compare Stored Embeddings – inspect stored vectors and understand how they are structured
 Update Documents and Track Embedding Changes – update content and observe embedding differences
 How Embedding Similarity Reflects Meaning – introduction to similarity-based comparison
 Prepare for Semantic Search – what to expect in the next tutorial

#ChromaDB #Embeddings #VectorDatabase #SemanticSearch #AIEmbeddings #VectorSearch #PythonAI

ChromaDB, embeddings in ChromaDB, store embeddings, view embeddings, update documents chromadb, embedding similarity, chromadb tutorial, vector database python, semantic search basics, how embeddings work
```

It was a dark and stormy night…no, really! I was innocently about to run the simplest of scripts — a snippet I found while following a course on using ChromaDB. It was so simple that it should have been trivial. And then — boom! An inexplicable error appeared, and when I lazily checked what had happened, it led me down a chain of strange errors and unexpected clues that eventually revealed a bigger truth: the ChromaDB Hugging Face embedding wrapper was calling a deprecated endpoint. This is the story of that night…

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*bvH3BCTWbG-vdme0CJqVpw.png)

Our little detective

## Embeddings by default and with Hugging Face

The first script was trivial, almost comical. Just created a temporal, non-persistent client, then a collection without specifying an embedding model, inserted a word (“hola”), and retrieved the embeddings.

```
import chromadb
chroma_client = chromadb.Client()

# Use the embedding model by default
collection = chroma_client.get_or_create_collection(name="test_default")

collection.add(documents=["hola"], ids=["1"])
results = collection.get(include=["embeddings", "documents"])

print (results)
print(results["embeddings"].shape)  # Size of embeddings array
```

It printed our results as

```
$ uv run embeddings_default.py
{'ids': ['1'], 'embeddings': array([[-6.51595369e-02,  9.27440152e-02, -2.62070056e-02,\
        -1.60606522e-02, -6.03321306e-02, -9.46351364e-02,......\
 2.16619601e-03,  3.44089046e-02,  4.92913201e-02]]), 'documents': ['hola'], 'uris': None, 'included': ['embeddings', 'documents'], 'data': None, 'metadatas': None}
(1, 384)
```

It was, after all, using the by-default model `sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2` which has 384 embedding dimensions.

But I wanted to be able to explicitly control what model to use. So I followed [ChromaDB’s documentation on Hugging Face Integrations](https://docs.trychroma.com/integrations/embedding-models/hugging-face), and created:

```
import chromadb
import chromadb.utils.embedding_functions as embedding_functions

HUGGINGFACE_KEY = "hf_MYHFKEYHERE"

huggingface_ef = embedding_functions.HuggingFaceEmbeddingFunction(
    api_key=HUGGINGFACE_KEY,
    model_name="sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2"
)

chroma_client = chromadb.Client()

# We explicitly set the embedding
collection = chroma_client.get_or_create_collection(
    name="test_huggingface",
    embedding_function=huggingface_ef
    )

collection.add(documents=["hola"], ids=["1"])
results = collection.get(include=["embeddings", "documents"])

print (results)
print(results["embeddings"].shape)
```

And then the case took a turn: an error emerged.

```
$ uv run embeddings_huggingWRONG.py
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/Bases_Datos/Chroma/Chroma_Embeddings/embeddings_huggingWRONG.py", line 22, in <module>
    collection.add(documents=["hola"], ids=["1"])
  File "/home/Bases_Datos/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/chromadb/api/models/Collection.py", line 86, in add
    add_request = self._validate_and_prepare_add_request(
                  ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/home/Bases_Datos/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/chromadb/utils/embedding_functions/huggingface_embedding_function.py", line 82, in __call__
    return [np.array(embedding, dtype=np.float32) for embedding in response]
            ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
ValueError: could not convert string to float: 'error' in add.
```

I thought, _oh no, not another error that is going to make me debug obscure internal functions…_ I was already about to serve myself a cup of coffee for an all-nighter, wondering how a simple script had suddenly turned into real work, when a thought occurred to me: ‘string to float’… is the string here literally ‘error’? Could the API be returning an error message instead of a vector of floats?

## The mystery of the unexpected string

Once I had the hypothesis and after a quick internet search, all kinds of reasons came out: “The hugging face inference API does not support this model!”, “You spelled your API parameter wrong”, “use another provider”(that gave me the biggest laugh next to “did you connect your network?” Ha!). Everything seemed dark and gloomy until I tried:

```
import requests
import numpy as np

HUGGINGFACE_KEY = "hf_MYHFKEYHERE"
API_URL = "https://api-inference.huggingface.co/pipeline/feature-extraction/sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2"
headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {HUGGINGFACE_KEY}"}

def query(texts):
    response = requests.post(API_URL, headers=headers, json={"inputs": texts})
    return response.json()

# Test the API directly
response = query(["hola"])
print("API Response:", response)

# Check if it's an error or valid embeddings
if isinstance(response, list) and all(isinstance(x, (list, np.ndarray)) for x in response):
    print("Valid embeddings received")
else:
    print("Error:", response)
```

, and I got this

```
API Response: {'error': 'https://api-inference.huggingface.co is no longer supported. Please use https://router.huggingface.co instead.'}
Error: {'error': 'https://api-inference.huggingface.co is no longer supported. Please use https://router.huggingface.co instead.'}
```

Bingo! Time to get into my pajamas and call it a night…

## Get Hitoruna’s stories in your inbox

Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer.

Subscribe

Subscribe

Remember me for faster sign in

Not so fast, Watson! — the plot was just thickening…

## Knocking on the wrong door

I tried to follow the advice above and did

```
import requests
import numpy as np

HUGGINGFACE_KEY = "hf_MYHFKEYHERE"
MODEL = "sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2"
API_URL = f"https://router.huggingface.co/pipeline/feature-extraction/{MODEL}"

headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {HUGGINGFACE_KEY}"}

def query(texts):
    payload = {"inputs": texts}
    r = requests.post(API_URL, headers=headers, json=payload)
    print("STATUS:", r.status_code)
    print("RAW RESPONSE:", r.text)
    return r.json()

# Test the API
response = query(["hola"])
print("API Response:", response)

# Check if embeddings returned
if isinstance(response, list) and isinstance(response[0], list):
    print("Valid embeddings received, vector length:", len(response[0]))
else:
    print("Error:", response)
```

Then I got

```
$ uv run debug_hfemb2.py
STATUS: 404
RAW RESPONSE: Not Found
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/Bases_Datos/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/requests/models.py", line 976, in json
    return complexjson.loads(self.text, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

  File "/home/Bases_Datos/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/requests/models.py", line 980, in json
    raise RequestsJSONDecodeError(e.msg, e.doc, e.pos)
requests.exceptions.JSONDecodeError: Expecting value: line 1 column 1 (char 0)
```

I had no idea what this could mean, and then I realized I had fortunately put those logs for status and raw response. The request had reached the server, but the server had nothing at the location to respond with. I was again knocking on the wrong door!

## Curl enters the crime scene.

I finally reached for the battered tool every engineer-detective keeps at the bottom of the toolbox — because it always gets results: curl.

```
$ curl -X POST https://router.huggingface.co/pipeline/feature-extraction \
>   -H "Authorization: Bearer hf_MYHFKEYHERE" \
>   -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
>   -d '{"inputs": ["hello world"], "model": "sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2"}'
Not Found
```

Yes. As suspected. With that in my hand, I did a quick search and found a [Hugging Face discussion](https://huggingface.co/sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2/discussions/116) opened on May 15. Turns out `feature-extraction` was undocumented! (what?) . But more importantly, the real up-to-date URL for the model is `https://router.huggingface.co/hf-inference/models/sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L66-V2/pipeline/feature-extraction`

```
$ curl -L \
>     -X POST \
>     -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
>     -H "Authorization: Bearer hf_MYHFKEYHERE" \
>     https://router.huggingface.co/hf-inference/models/sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2/pipeline/feature-extraction \
>     -d '{"inputs": ["hello"] }'
[[-0.0627717748284339....\
4,0.007092175539582968]]
```

Excellent!

## Checking that it works

I rewrote my checking script as

```
import requests

HUGGINGFACE_KEY = "hf_MYHFKEYHERE"  # Replace with your actual key
MODEL = "sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2"

# CORRECT VERIFIED ENDPOINT
API_URL = f"https://router.huggingface.co/hf-inference/models/{MODEL}/pipeline/feature-extraction"

headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {HUGGINGFACE_KEY}"}

def query(texts):
    payload = {"inputs": texts}
    response = requests.post(API_URL, headers=headers, json=payload)
    print("STATUS:", response.status_code)

    if response.status_code == 200:
        return response.json()
    else:
        print("ERROR:", response.text)
        return None

# Test the API
response = query(["hola"])
print("API Response:", response)

if response and isinstance(response, list):
    print(f"Success! Got {len(response)} embeddings")
    if len(response) > 0:
        print(f"Vector length: {len(response[0])}")
```

and got

```
$ uv run debug_hfemb4.py
STATUS: 200
API Response: [[-0.06515944004058838 ....\
 0.04929133504629135]]
Success! Got 1 embeddings
Vector length: 384
```

## Writing a custom class for ChromaDB

So all that remained was to fix our original “simple” script — that small, innocent-looking little snippet that somehow led me on a full-blown nighttime adventure. To do that, I decided to write a custom class so that I can use it the same way as it was written in the ChromaDB Integrations

```
# chromacustom.py
import requests
import numpy as np
from chromadb.api.types import EmbeddingFunction

class HuggingFaceRouterEmbeddingFunction(EmbeddingFunction):

    def __init__(self, api_key, model_name):
        self.api_key = api_key
        self.model_name = model_name

        # Correct updated endpoint
        self.url = (
            f"https://router.huggingface.co/hf-inference/models/"
            f"{model_name}/pipeline/feature-extraction"
        )

        self.headers = {
            "Authorization": f"Bearer {self.api_key}",
            "Content-Type": "application/json"
        }

    def __call__(self, texts):
        payload = {"inputs": texts}

        r = requests.post(self.url, headers=self.headers, json=payload)

        if r.status_code != 200:
            raise RuntimeError(
                f"HuggingFace API error {r.status_code}: {r.text}"
            )

        data = r.json()

        # Return as float32 numpy arrays (what Chroma expects)
        return [np.array(vec, dtype=np.float32) for vec in data]
```

and then use it in my simple snippet:

```
import chromadb
from chromacustom import HuggingFaceRouterEmbeddingFunction

HUGGINGFACE_KEY = "hf_MYHFKEYHERE"

huggingface_ef = HuggingFaceRouterEmbeddingFunction(
    api_key=HUGGINGFACE_KEY,
    model_name="sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2"
)

chroma_client = chromadb.Client()
collection = chroma_client.get_or_create_collection(
    name="test_huggingface",
    embedding_function=huggingface_ef
    )

collection.add(documents=["hola"], ids=["1"])
results = collection.get(include=["embeddings", "documents"])

print (results)
print(results["embeddings"].shape)  # Size of embeddings array
```

And with that

```
$ uv run embeddings_hugging.py
{'ids': ['1'], 'embeddings': array([[-6.51594400e-02,  9.27440375e-02, -2.62070242e-02,\
        -1.60606895e-02\
 4.92913350e-02]]), 'documents': ['hola'], 'uris': None, 'included': ['embeddings', 'documents'], 'data': None, 'metadatas': None}
(1, 384)
```

## Epilogue

The case was solved. I had managed to solve not one but a double mu…. deprecation. 😝. I tested five other embedding models: `all-mpnet-base-v2` , `all-MiniLM-L12-v2` , `paraphrase-multilingual-miniLM-L12-v2` , `all-distilroberta-v1` and `paraphrase-MiniLM-L6-v2` — All of them worked perfectly. It was finally time to set down my trusty debugging magnifying glass and call it a night, satisfied. Outside, the night has turned calm and pleasant — for now. Somewhere out there, the next deprecation might already be plotting its move.

If you enjoyed this little debugging adventure, feel free to clap👏, **follow,** and **share** — it really helps!

You can also check out my [previous story](https://medium.com/gopenai/pinecone-with-hugging-face-6b22decbcf4a) on vector databases and Hugging Face, and stay tuned for upcoming posts on ML, RAG, MLOps, and more. Till the next time!.

## [​](https://docs.trychroma.com/docs/overview/getting-started\#install-manually)  Install Manually

1

[Navigate to header](https://docs.trychroma.com/docs/overview/getting-started#)

### Install

pip

poetry

uv

```
pip install chromadb
```

2

[Navigate to header](https://docs.trychroma.com/docs/overview/getting-started#)

### Create a Chroma Client

Python

```
import chromadb
chroma_client = chromadb.Client()
```

3

[Navigate to header](https://docs.trychroma.com/docs/overview/getting-started#)

### Create a collection

Collections are where you’ll store your embeddings, documents, and any additional metadata. Collections index your embeddings and documents, and enable efficient retrieval and filtering. You can create a collection with a name:

Python

```
collection = chroma_client.create_collection(name="my_collection")
```

4

[Navigate to header](https://docs.trychroma.com/docs/overview/getting-started#)

### Add some text documents to the collection

Chroma will store your text and handle embedding and indexing automatically. You can also customize the embedding model. You must provide unique string IDs for your documents.

Python

```
collection.add(
    ids=["id1", "id2"],
    documents=[\
        "This is a document about pineapple",\
        "This is a document about oranges"\
    ]
)
```

5

[Navigate to header](https://docs.trychroma.com/docs/overview/getting-started#)

### Query the collection

You can query the collection with a list of query texts, and Chroma will return the n most similar results. It’s that easy!

Python

```
results = collection.query(
    query_texts=["This is a query document about hawaii"], # Chroma will embed this for you
    n_results=2 # how many results to return
)
print(results)
```

If n\_results is not provided, Chroma will return 10 results by default. Here we only added 2 documents, so we set n\_results=2.

6

[Navigate to header](https://docs.trychroma.com/docs/overview/getting-started#)

### Inspect Results

From the above - you can see that our query about hawaii is semantically most similar to the document about pineapple.

Python

```
{
  'documents': [[\
      'This is a document about pineapple',\
      'This is a document about oranges'\
  ]],
  'ids': [['id1', 'id2']],
  'distances': [[1.0404009819030762, 1.243080496788025]],
  'uris': None,
  'data': None,
  'metadatas': [[None, None]],
  'embeddings': None,
}
```

7

[Navigate to header](https://docs.trychroma.com/docs/overview/getting-started#)

### Try it out yourself

What if we tried querying with “This is a document about florida”? Here is a full example.

Python

```
import chromadb
chroma_client = chromadb.Client()

# switch \`create_collection\` to \`get_or_create_collection\` to avoid creating a new collection every time
collection = chroma_client.get_or_create_collection(name="my_collection")

# switch \`add\` to \`upsert\` to avoid adding the same documents every time
collection.upsert(
    documents=[\
        "This is a document about pineapple",\
        "This is a document about oranges"\
    ],
    ids=["id1", "id2"]
)

results = collection.query(
    query_texts=["This is a query document about florida"], # Chroma will embed this for you
    n_results=2 # how many results to return
)

print(results)
```

### Create a collection

Collections are where you’ll store your embeddings, documents, and any additional metadata. Collections index your embeddings and documents, and enable efficient retrieval and filtering. You can create a collection with a name:

TypeScript

```
const collection = await client.createCollection({
  name: "my_collection",
});
```

### Add some text documents to the collection

Chroma will store your text and handle embedding and indexing automatically. You can also customize the embedding model. You must provide unique string IDs for your documents.

TypeScript

```
await collection.add({
  ids: ["id1", "id2"],
  documents: [\
    "This is a document about pineapple",\
    "This is a document about oranges",\
  ],
});
```

### Query the collection

You can query the collection with a list of query texts, and Chroma will return the n most similar results. It’s that easy!

TypeScript

```
const results = await collection.query({
  queryTexts: ["This is a query document about hawaii"], // Chroma will embed this for you
  nResults: 2, // how many results to return
});

console.log(results);
```

If n\_results is not provided, Chroma will return 10 results by default. Here we only added 2 documents, so we set n\_results=2.

### Try it out yourself

What if we tried querying with “This is a document about florida”? Here is a full example.

TypeScript

```
import { ChromaClient } from "chromadb";
const client = new ChromaClient();

// switch `createCollection` to `getOrCreateCollection` to avoid creating a new collection every time
const collection = await client.getOrCreateCollection({
  name: "my_collection",
});

// switch `addRecords` to `upsertRecords` to avoid adding the same documents every time
await collection.upsert({
  documents: [\
    "This is a document about pineapple",\
    "This is a document about oranges",\
  ],
  ids: ["id1", "id2"],
});

const results = await collection.query({
  queryTexts: ["This is a query document about florida"], // Chroma will embed this for you
  nResults: 2, // how many results to return
});

console.log(results);
```

## [​](https://docs.trychroma.com/docs/overview/getting-started\#create-a-chroma-client)  Create a Chroma Client

Run the Chroma backend:

```
chroma run --path ./getting-started
```

Then create a client which connects to it:

```
use chroma::ChromaHttpClient;

let client = ChromaHttpClient::new(Default::default());
```

## [​](https://docs.trychroma.com/docs/overview/getting-started\#create-a-collection)  Create a collection

```
let collection = client
    .create_collection("my_collection", None, None)
    .await?;
```

## [​](https://docs.trychroma.com/docs/overview/getting-started\#add-some-text-documents-to-the-collection)  Add some text documents to the collection

The Rust client expects embeddings to be provided directly. Generate embeddings with your provider SDK, then pass them along with documents.

```
let embeddings = vec![vec![0.1, 0.2, 0.3], vec![0.4, 0.5, 0.6]];

collection
    .add(
        vec!["id1".to_string(), "id2".to_string()],
        embeddings,
        Some(vec![\
            Some("This is a document about pineapple".to_string()),\
            Some("This is a document about oranges".to_string()),\
        ]),
        None,
        None,
    )
    .await?;
```

## [​](https://docs.trychroma.com/docs/overview/getting-started\#query-the-collection)  Query the collection

```
let results = collection
    .query(vec![vec![0.1, 0.2, 0.3]], Some(2), None, None, None)
    .await?;
```
